newsitem.title: USA: Push for highway funds stalls U.S. budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Push for highway funds stalls U.S. budget deal.

text.p: Nervous House Republican leaders called a late-night meeting Tuesday to try to salvage the balanced budget agreement after lawmakers in both parties sought to boost funds for highways and transit.

White House budget director Franklin Raines said approval of an amendment earmarking $13 billion for transportation over five years, paid for with reductions in spending and tax cuts, could breach the budget pact worked out over the past four months.
Republican leaders summoned their colleagues to a meeting in an effort to head off passage of the changes and salvage the deal.

"The adminstration strongly opposes the amendment. ... If adopted this amendment would be a breach of the bipartisan (budget) agreement," Raines wrote to House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, a Republican from Ohio.

On the other side, 49 governors wrote the House urging more funds for transportation. The budget provides $124 billion for highways and mass transit, including the Amtrak passenger train line, through 2002. The increase they have sought would equal the amount paid each year by motorists in federal fuel taxes.

Democrat Nick Rahall of West Virginia, an author of the transportation amendment, told his colleagues their requests for special construction and repair projects would probably go unfilled if the budget pact was passed as originally written. "You can't build a bridge to the future without funding," Representative Corrine Brown, a Florida Democrat, said.

Transportation Committee chairman Bud Shuster, a Pennsylvania Republican, argued that the full House should have the right to adjust spending. "What are we, potted plants? Can't we as members of Congress make modest adjustments (in the budget)?" he asked.

Earlier in the day, White House officials had said they were confident of winning a majority of President Clinton's own Democratic Party despite a decision by House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt to vote against the budget.
The Missouri Democrat told the House he could not vote for a budget that shrank Medicare for the elderly while providing tax cuts for the wealthy.
"I refuse to be a party to an agreement that balances the budget in name only," he said. "I don't believe this budget is fair. I don't believe it invests properly in the future of our country."

The House was to vote on the balanced budget late in the day, while the Senate was expected to debate the proposal until a vote Thursday. Leaders of both chambers expect the measure will pass. But before that point is reached, many lawmakers will seek to change the budget or to offer alternatives.
The budget slows the growth of government spending for the next five years, cuts Medicare by $115 billion and brings the deficit down to zero by 2002 from this year's forecast level of $67 billion.

It also provides a net $85 billion tax cut. Raines said Republican leaders had given assurances that the cut would largely benefit families with children and those in which students are seeking post-secondary education.

But Gephardt said Republicans had forced acceptance of the tax cut in return for support for a balanced budget. "At a time when we are asking average, hard-working Americans to tighten their belts, we shouldn't be telling the wealthiest Americans that, not only don't they have to participate, they'll actually get a huge tax cut," he said.

Under the Republican tax proposals that will be before the tax-writing committees, Gephardt said, the wealthiest 1 percent of the country will see taxes reduced by $6,784 per person per year. Members of this group earn an average of $645,000 a year, he said.
Gephardt also argued that the tax cuts would cause the deficit to explode after 2002.

The cut of $85 billion is a small fraction of the nearly $10 trillion in taxes to be collected by the government from individuals and businesses over the next five years. At the same time, the government will spend $1.6 trillion in fiscal 1997, rising to $1.9 trillion in fiscal 2002.

Congressional budget committees said that over its five years, the plan cut $304 billion in spending from what would have occurred without changes in policy but gave Clinton $33 billion to spend on education, the environment and other domestic priorities.
